title: Ink on the Water
subtitle: The Lanternweald — expansion pass two
content:
The sea returned a piece of paper on a morning when nobody had asked it for anything.

Maui found it caught between two stones below the repaired landing. He was looking for a replacement mooring ring, which was a sensible task. Finding a soaking-wet fragment of the Lanternweald's oldest ledger did not belong on his list.

"Treasure," he declared when he carried it up the steps.

"That is a piece of rubbish."

"Treasure frequently begins as rubbish to people with no imagination."

"It smells like fish."

"An authentic sea treasure."

He laid it on the workbench. The paper was thick, almost cloth, with an edge blackened by an old burn. Pale ink ran between two columns of dates. Most of the writing had dissolved.

Near the bottom there was a drawing of a key.

A brass key with a tiny half-moon notch.

My fingers moved to the blue thread at my throat before I could stop them.

Maui noticed.

"What is it?"

I pulled out my key and held it beside the drawing.

His grin vanished.

"Oh."

"Yes."

He leaned close, careful not to touch the damaged paper. The notch matched, right down to a small nick along the lower tooth.

"That means this was yours."

"Does it?"

He straightened.

I studied the drawing again. There was no name. No address. Nothing to prove the paper had been written about me rather than about whoever had owned a similar key before I arrived.

"It's a drawing," I said. "We don't know who made it."

"But it looks exactly like—"

"I know."

My voice came out sharper than I intended. Maui stepped back.

"I wasn't trying to decide for you."

"I know." I swallowed. "I'm sorry."

He watched me, the hurt in his eyes giving way to worry.

"Do you want to put it away?"

"Not yet."

We dried the page between clean sheets in Tamsin's workshop. She weighed the corners with smooth stones and forbade Maui from breathing heroically near it.

Maui hovered over the workbench until Tamsin pointed at a chalk line on the floor.

"Behind that."

"That line was drawn for children."

"Then you should understand it easily."

I made a sound that came out halfway between a cough and a laugh. Mini Maui rolled down his arm, pressed his own palms to an imaginary pane of glass, and stared at the ledger like a tiny impatient museum visitor.

Maui nudged him back toward his shoulder. "I'm excellent at solving ancient mysteries."

"You're excellent at dropping sand on wet paper," Tamsin replied.

"One time."

"Today."

He threw his arms wide in injured magnificence, but his eyes kept returning to the torn corner of the ledger. People had once written down who was allowed to leave. No amount of muscle could make the missing words reappear.

After several minutes he sat on a stool behind the line. He still whispered spectacular theories to me whenever Tamsin turned away. Some were nonsense. A few made me ask better questions. He wasn't suddenly a scholar; he was a curious trickster who hated a puzzle he couldn't wrestle.

"I don't breathe heroically."

"You are doing it now," she said.

We waited.

The sunlight moved across the room. Beyond the open shutter, people crossed Lanternwell Square carrying market baskets. The new departure register lay on Neri's desk. A child had already asked whether the crab on the tide sign was a guardian spirit.

Maui had said yes.

I had said no.

The child had decided it was a guardian spirit of checking the tide.

By noon, enough of the page had dried for Tamsin to lift it. A second drawing emerged beside the key: a stone arch with seven short scratches along its underside.

"The well has only six," I said.

Tamsin looked at me.

"Are you sure?"

"I counted them when we hung the festival lanterns."

"Then perhaps you should count again."

I disliked reasonable advice when it involved climbing ladders.

Neri found us at the well.

They took one look at the page and went still.

I had seen people frightened. This was different. They looked like someone whose childhood had come through the door without knocking.

"Where did you get that?"

"At the cove," Maui said. "Between the south stones."

Neri held out their hands.

I almost gave it to them immediately. It seemed kinder.

Then I remembered Lark asking to leave without explanation. The way Neri had said we used to close them in storms and then refused to describe who could leave.

"Can we look at it together?" I asked.

Neri's hands fell.

"Yes."

We took the page to Moonroot Archive, where the workroom had a dry slate table and a window that faced the spring. A librarian brought a low lamp. Iroh, who had stopped by to return a borrowed history, offered tea and then, after looking at Neri's face, quietly left it on a side table.

No one turned the scene into a performance.

Neri traced the burnt edge without touching it.

"This is from the old maintenance ledger."

"Why was it in the water?" I asked.

"Not everything burned stays burned. There was a flood."

"When?"

"Before the new Threadways."

"Before me?"

They nodded.

I turned the page slightly. Beneath the key was a number written in narrow, fading strokes. Twelve.

"Is that a date?"

"No." Neri's voice grew quiet. "A measurement. Twelve feet from the old waterline."

Maui looked toward the window.

"The spring?"

"Under it."

There was a long silence.

"So the key isn't necessarily mine," I said.

Neri met my eyes.

"No. It belonged to people who maintained the drainage path."

"People, plural?"

"More than one keeper held that pattern."

Relief and disappointment arrived together. Both were uncomfortable. Neither was a reason to demand a different answer.

"Why would the drains be locked?" Maui asked.

Neri looked down at their walking stick.

"Because someone was afraid of what might happen if a door stayed open."

A thin current of anger went through me.

"Which door?"

Neri did not answer.

I could have pushed. Part of me wanted to. I'd spent so long with gaps in my memory that any missing piece felt personal. A scrap of paper with my key on it seemed like an invitation to make the entire valley's history about myself.

Instead, I placed the page between two protective sheets.

"We should record what we actually know," I said. "Found at the cove. Drawing of a maintenance key. Old waterline. An arch that doesn't match the one outside."

Maui leaned against the table.

"And what we don't know?"

"That too."

Neri looked at me for a long moment. Then they nodded.

"I can tell you where the older diagrams are kept," they said. "I am not ready to tell you everything that happened."

"That's your choice," I answered. "But we need to know whether the old structure is dangerous."

"It may be."

"Then we need people qualified to inspect it, whether you're ready for the story or not."

Neri's face changed. Not pleased, exactly. More like someone recognizing a door they'd hoped never to open.

Outside the archive, Maui and I walked along the canal. The stones were warm. A few late flowers clung to the cracks between them.

"You're angry," he said.

"A little."

"At Neri?"

"At the part where everybody's safety depends on a story no one wants to tell."

He nodded.

"Would you have wanted them to say it all?"

"Yes. No. I don't know." I touched the key again. "I want the past to make sense. But I don't want the past to own me."

Maui stopped beside the bridge.

"You know what I think?"

"I anticipate a very dramatic answer."

"I think you can be curious without being a prisoner."

"That was suspiciously reasonable."

"I occasionally produce wisdom by accident."

He took my hand. My thumb followed a scar across his knuckles. His expression softened, and he stepped closer.

"Still want to look at the drawings tomorrow?" he asked.

"With proper tools, yes."

"Still want me there?"

"Yes."

He kissed my forehead. For a moment the canal and the lost ledger and the question of who first held my key became small enough to carry.

That evening I went back to the well alone and counted the scratches.

One. Two. Three. Four. Five. Six.

The seventh was not scratched into the arch.

It was hidden on the underside of a stone below the lantern hooks, visible only when I crouched and looked from the water's edge.

I did not pry it open. I did not call for Maui to lift the stone with heroic ease.

I drew what I saw and wrote down the angle of the light.

Then I went home and put my key beside my notebook.

Some mysteries were worth approaching carefully.

That did not mean they would wait forever.
